topic: laying an overgrown hawthorn hedge in winter: pleaching the stems, driving stakes and binding the top

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: kolo pomiarowe do odmierzania lancuchow zywoplotu

base: I am laying an overgrown hawthorn hedge along the bottom of a wet meadow.
A blackthorn hedge runs along the top of the field and has never been laid.
I bought a measuring wheel last autumn, because pacing out the chains never came out right.
The stems are thick as my wrist and many have gone hollow at the base.
Should I coppice the worst of them, or try to pleach the whole length?
Pleach whatever will bend, because a coppiced stool takes seven years to make a hedge.
A hollow stem still carries sap up one side of its rim.
Cut low and long, leaving a hinge no thicker than your little finger.
The hinge is what keeps the stem alive once it lies over.
I cut low and long and most of the stems came over willingly.
The measuring wheel says I have laid about forty yards so far.
Three of the thickest stems split right down the hinge as they went over.
Was my cut too shallow, or did I push them over too fast?
Your cut was too shallow, since a thick stem needs almost the whole trunk removed.
Leave only a strip of bark and a thin sliver of wood behind.
Push the stem down slowly with your knee while the billhook stays in the cut.
A split hinge dies within a season and leaves a gap forever.
I cut deeper on the thick stems and not one of them has split since.
The measuring wheel now reads ninety yards of finished hedge along the meadow.
That blackthorn hedge at the top grows far denser than mine ever has.
Would blackthorn lay as easily, or does it need different handling altogether?
Blackthorn lays well enough, though it suckers freely and will spread into the field.
Its wood is brittle and the thorns punish any careless hand terribly.
Cut it in hard frost when the sap is down and the stems bend.
Hawthorn forgives a poor cut, but blackthorn snaps and leaves you nothing.
I have finished the pleaching and now need to drive the stakes in.
I cut hazel from the copse but some rods look rather thin and whippy.
The old boy down the lane insists on ash stakes for wet ground.
Does the wood really matter, or is any straight rod good enough?
The wood matters greatly, because a stake must hold for a full seven years.
Hazel rots quickly in wet ground and often snaps under the weight of binding.
Ash holds far longer and drives without splitting even in heavy clay.
Set them a yard apart and drive them well below the pleachers.
I cut ash stakes and drove them a yard apart the whole way along.
The binders went on last week and the top is now firm and even.
Rabbits have begun nibbling the new shoots wherever the hedge sits low.
Should I fence the whole length, or will the hedge outgrow the damage?
Fence it for two seasons, because rabbits will keep a young hedge flat forever.
New growth comes from the hinge and cannot afford to be eaten twice.
A simple wire net along the field side will be quite enough.
Take it down once the shoots stand higher than a rabbit can reach.
